title: Capitals for Names, Days and I
keyIdea: Names start with a capital letter: names of people (Sam, Mia), places (Leeds, London) and pets (Rex). The days of the week are names too, so Monday and Sunday start with a capital, but sunny and morning do not. The word I, meaning me, is always a capital, even in the middle of a sentence. Ordinary words such as dog, park and town stay small, and so do words that just contain an i, such as in and it.
familyTip: Write a shopping list or a birthday card together and hunt for the names: people, places, pets and days. Your child gives each one a big first letter. Then ask, 'Who is I?' and check every I in the card is a capital. If they write Dog, ask, 'Is that its name, or what it is?'

visual.caption: Does the word need a capital letter, or does it stay small? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort names from ordinary words, tap the names in sentences, stamp capitals on day names, fix the lone i and fill a postcard.

kid: Names start with a big letter. It is called a capital letter. Sam, Mia and Raj are names. So are Leeds and London.
Words that are not names stay small. dog, park and girl are not names. But if your dog is called Rex, Rex gets a capital.
The days of the week are names too. Monday, Friday and Sunday all start with a capital. But sunny and morning stay small.
When you write about you, use I. It is always a big I, even in the middle. Mum and I went in. But in and it stay small.
adult: Ages 5 to 7. The National Curriculum in England asks Year 1 pupils to use a capital letter for names of people, places, the days of the week and the personal pronoun I (Year 1 writing, with 'capital letters for names and for the personal pronoun I' in English Appendix 2). Spelling the days of the week is also on the Year 1 list. Common Core L.1.2a asks first graders to capitalize dates and names of people.

The grammar idea behind this is the proper noun: the name of one particular person, place, pet or day, as opposed to a common noun such as dog, town or day. Rex the dog and the city of Leeds get capitals; a dog and a town do not. Months and festivals follow the same rule, and children meet them soon after.

Common mistakes: no capital on a name (sam), a small i for the pronoun, capitals on ordinary nouns that feel important (Dog, Park), a capital on every word in a line, and a capital on words that only contain the letter i (In, It). Some children also mix up sunny with Sunday or treat morning as the name of a day.

In the lab your child sorts eight words into names and ordinary words, taps the names in four sentences, drags a capital stamp onto day names but not onto sunny, morning or week, fixes the lone i in three lines, and fills in a postcard where one word, dog, must stay small.

practice.hint: Check the word I and the name.
practice.explain: I is always a capital, and Sam is a name, so it starts with a capital S.

practice.prompt: A class list has {b} boys' names and {g} girls' names. How many names need a capital letter?
practice.hint: Every name on the list starts with a capital.
practice.explain: {b} and {g} make {=b+g} names, and every one needs a capital.

practice.prompt: Which word needs a capital letter?
practice.hint: Which one is the name of a day?
practice.explain: Tuesday is a day of the week, so it is a name: Tuesday. teacher and table stay small.

practice.prompt: Ben writes the word I {n} times in his diary. {k} of them are a small i. How many does he need to fix?
practice.hint: Only the small ones need fixing.
practice.explain: Only the small ones are wrong, so he fixes {k}. Every I meaning me must be a capital.

choices: My dog Rex likes the park.
My Dog Rex likes the park.
My dog rex likes the Park.
practice.hint: Only the name gets a capital. dog and park are not names.
practice.explain: Rex is the dog's name, so it gets a capital. dog and park are ordinary words, so they stay small.

pool.prompt: Why does Leeds start with a capital letter?
choices: It is the name of a place
It is a thing you can see
pool.hint: Is it a name, or just a kind of thing?
pool.explain: Leeds is the name of a city, so it starts with a capital. town would stay small.

pool.hint: Check the day and the word I.
pool.explain: Monday is a day name and I means me, so both need a capital.

pool.prompt: There are 7 days in a week. Mia has written {k} of them with a capital. How many more need a capital?
pool.hint: Every day name needs one. Take away the ones she has done.
pool.explain: 7 days take away {k} done leaves {=7-k} more to fix.

pool.prompt: Which word should NOT have a capital letter?
pool.hint: Which one is not the name of a day or a person?
pool.explain: morning is a time of day, not a name, so it stays small. Friday and Mia are names.

pool.hint: I is always big. and is not a name.
pool.explain: I is always a capital. and is an ordinary word, so it stays small.

pool.prompt: We saw raj at the shop. Which word needs a capital?
pool.hint: Find the person's name. shop and saw are not names.
pool.explain: Raj is a person's name: We saw Raj at the shop. shop and saw are not names.

pool.prompt: A postcard has {a} names in it and uses the word I {b} times. How many capital letters do these words need?
pool.hint: Each name needs one, and each I is a capital.
pool.explain: {a} names and {b} times I make {=a+b} capitals.

pool.prompt: Which one is the name of a day?
pool.explain: Sunday is a day of the week, so it is a name with a capital. sunny and sunshine are about the weather.

pool.hint: in and is have an i inside, but they are not I.
pool.explain: Only I on its own gets a capital. in and is stay small.

pool.prompt: Your dog is called Bella. How do you write her name?
pool.hint: A pet's name is still a name.
pool.explain: A pet's name is a name, so it starts with a capital: Bella.
